title: Deterministic FPTAS for the nonnegative permanent
formal:
Does there exist one finite deterministic algorithm \(D\) and integers \(C,k\ge1\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\), every explicitly encoded matrix \(A\in\mathbb Q_{\ge0}^{n\times n}\), and every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), \(D(A,\varepsilon)\) halts within
\[C\bigl(L+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+1\bigr)^{k}\]
Turing-machine steps and returns a nonnegative rational \(z\) satisfying
\[(1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{per}(A)\le z\le(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{per}(A)?\]
Here \(L\) is the full binary input length, and the permanent is defined below. The guarantee must hold on every input without randomness.
definitions:
Let \([n]=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) and let \(S_{n}\) be the set of bijections from \([n]\) to itself. For a nonnegative rational matrix define
\[\operatorname{per}(A)=\sum_{\pi\in S_{n}}\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}A_{i,\pi(i)}.\]
Zero entries, zero rows, reducible matrices and arbitrarily large or small positive rational entries are permitted. There is no density, expansion, degree, rank, stochastic-scaling, or positive-entry lower-bound promise. This is the usual unsigned permutation sum, not the determinant or the hafnian. For a zero–one matrix it counts perfect matchings in the bipartite graph having one vertex for each row and each column, with an edge exactly where the entry is one. For a weighted matrix, each matching contributes the product of its edge weights.

For an integer \(t\ge0\), let \(b(t)\) be its ordinary binary expansion, with \(b(0)=0\), and set \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\). Encode \(n\) as \(E(n)\), then encode all \(n^{2}\) entries in row-major order. Each entry is a reduced pair \(u/v\), with integers \(u\ge0,v\ge1\), encoded by \(E(u)E(v)\). Encode \(\varepsilon=r/s\) in lowest terms, \(0<r<s\), by appending \(E(r)E(s)\). The length of this complete string is \(L\). It is not a succinct circuit or oracle description of a larger matrix. Output \(E(p)E(q)\), with \(p\ge0,q\ge1\), represents \(z=p/q\); the output need not be reduced.

Computation uses one finite deterministic multitape Turing machine, a read-only input tape, finitely many work tapes over fixed finite alphabets and an output tape. Each transition costs one step, including all arithmetic, reading, writing, storage and output costs. There are no random bits, advice strings, oracles or unit-cost exact-real operations. The machine and the two clock constants are independent of the dimension, entries and requested accuracy. The exponent is fixed independently of \(\varepsilon\); polynomial dependence on the numerical value of \(1/\varepsilon\) is permitted in addition to dependence on its encoding length. No guarantee is required on malformed inputs.

The approximation is relative to the permanent itself, not additive relative to \(n!\), a matrix norm, or a rescaled quantity. Nonnegativity makes the permanent positive precisely when the positive-entry bipartite support graph has a perfect matching. Thus the zero case is deterministically recognizable in polynomial time, and the displayed inequality requires \(z=0\) exactly in that case. Arbitrarily small positive permanents must still receive the same relative guarantee. This is a genuine algorithm-existence question, not a numerical-value target at the catalogue’s absolute \(1/100\) tolerance.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify the finite deterministic machine and constants \(C,k\), and prove termination, the full bit-cost bound, the rational output and both inequalities for every valid nonnegative rational matrix and every valid accuracy. A negative answer must rule out every such machine and clock, rather than just one approximation formula or family of algorithms. A conditional lower bound remains conditional unless its hypothesis is also proved. A randomized FPRAS, a scheme restricted to positive dense matrices, a fixed dimension-dependent approximation factor, or running time \(n^{h(1/\varepsilon)}\) with an unbounded accuracy-dependent exponent does not qualify. Exact #P-hardness alone is not a negative answer: an exponentially small requested error may legitimately require exponential time under an FPTAS clock.
why: A landmark derandomization problem: match the accuracy and efficiency of the permanent FPRAS using deterministic computation on every nonnegative rational matrix.

importance.reason: One of the central explicit tests of derandomization in approximate counting, with broad connections to matchings, sampling, convex optimization and correlation decay.

progress.text: Jerrum–Sinclair–Vigoda establish the nonnegative permanent FPRAS; the checked author-hosted manuscript is the STOC 2001 version and the journal article appeared in 2004.
Anari–Rezaei prove the tight \(2^{n/2}\) Bethe comparison; arXiv first posting 7 November 2018, checked v2 dated 9 December 2019, FOCS 2019.
Chen–Vigoda–Yang v1 reports a faster randomized permanent approximation with explicit error and failure-probability dependence.
Anari posts the claimed deterministic \(c^{n}\) improvement for some \(c<\sqrt2\); the checked current version is v2 of 1 September.
Narang–Perkins v1 independently claims an improvement below the same exponential base.
Yi v1 claims a deterministic FPTAS under fixed positive density and nonzero-weight margins.
Kudria–Luo–Majid v1 reports general deterministic polynomial-time approximation with a subexponential factor and explicitly distinguishes it from an FPTAS.

status_note: Individually checked on 14 September 2026. The current Kudria–Luo–Majid v1 of 9 September explicitly distinguishes its subexponential-factor approximation from an FPTAS; Narang–Perkins v1 also identifies the FPTAS as unknown even for zero–one matrices. Anari v2 (1 September), Narang–Perkins v1 (31 August), the randomized Chen–Vigoda–Yang v1 (27 August), and Yi v1 (3 September, fixed-density and weight margins) report narrower advances. Their statements, versions and relevant model restrictions were checked, but complete new proofs and any linked Lean formalization were not independently verified. Bounded later-work checks found no matching unrestricted deterministic FPTAS. Retained as source_open with these limits; exact #P-hardness does not establish a negative answer.

context_blocks.text: The permanent is a basic counting polynomial whose nonnegative entries remove cancellation. Its zero–one specialization counts bipartite perfect matchings, while weighted inputs total the contributions of all such matchings. Existence of a matching and accurate estimation of their total weight are different tasks. The input’s full bit encoding matters when weights vary over many orders of magnitude; floating-point proximity to zero is not a substitute for the required relative guarantee.

Jerrum, Sinclair and Vigoda establish a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme for all nonnegative matrices. This makes the permanent a particularly explicit test of the power of randomness: the desired relative approximation is already possible with bounded error, and the question asks whether it can always be obtained deterministically with the same fully polynomial dependence on inverse accuracy.

Anari and Rezaei prove the tight comparison \(\operatorname{Bethe}(A)\le\operatorname{per}(A)\le2^{n/2}\operatorname{Bethe}(A)\). Here the Bethe permanent is a particular variational estimate over nonnegative matrices with all row and column sums equal to one. Block diagonal matrices with \(2\times2\) all-ones blocks attain the factor. This proves a limitation of that estimate, not a lower bound on all deterministic approximation algorithms. The result was first posted in 2018 and presented at FOCS 2019; the journal’s later issue date does not make it a new 2025 algorithm.

Chen, Vigoda and Yang’s 27 August 2026 preprint reports an improved permanent FPRAS, with \(O(n^{6}\varepsilon^{-2}\log^{5}n\log(2/\delta))\) time for zero–one inputs of dimension at least two, where \(\delta\) is the failure probability. The theorem also states an extension to nonnegative matrices. This is a reported improvement on the randomized side; it does not remove randomness or establish this deterministic target.

Anari’s preprint, first posted on 28 August 2026 and revised on 1 September, claims a deterministic polynomial-time factor \(c^{n}\) for an absolute \(c<\sqrt2\). Its main theorem explicitly treats rational matrices, with zero entries and certified finite precision discussed in Appendix A. Narang and Perkins independently claim the same type of improvement in their 31 August preprint. These are bounds for estimates different from the unmodified Bethe value, so they do not contradict its tight example. The new proofs and any associated formalization were not independently checked in full by this review.

Kudria, Luo and Majid’s 9 September 2026 preprint states a stronger general result: positive rational endpoints \(L_{A}\le\operatorname{per}(A)\le U_{A}\), after separate zero detection, with
\[\log(U_{A}/L_{A})=O\!\left(\frac{n(\log\log n)^{2}}{\log n}\right)\]
as \(n\to\infty\), using a polynomial number of bit operations on arbitrary nonnegative rational inputs. This is a subexponential multiplicative interval width, not subexponential running time. Its Theorem 1.2 makes the error/time tradeoff explicit, and the introduction still distinguishes its guarantee from a fully polynomial relative approximation scheme. The full new proof has not been independently verified here.

Yi’s preprint of 3 September 2026 claims a deterministic FPTAS on another substantial subdomain: nonzero matrix entries must lie in \([\theta,1]\), and every row and column of the support must contain at least \((1/2+\gamma)n\) nonzero entries, for fixed \(\theta>0\) and \(\gamma>0\). Its polynomial exponents may depend on those margins. The statement includes some matrices with zeros, but it does not cover unrestricted rational inputs or margins that shrink with the input size. Its full proof was not independently verified in this review.

The remaining question is a uniform relative approximation guarantee with a fixed polynomial running-time exponent and arbitrary requested accuracy. Improving an exponential factor, making its logarithm sublinear in dimension, and solving a restricted dense case are all meaningful advances, but none of their stated guarantees is the full requirement. A resolution would settle a central concrete derandomization problem in approximate counting.

sentences: The permanent of a nonnegative matrix sums the weights of all perfect matchings in its bipartite support graph.
The question asks for one deterministic algorithm approximating this value to any requested relative accuracy on every nonnegative rational matrix.
Its running time must be polynomial in the full binary input length and inverse accuracy, with a fixed exponent and exact output zero when the permanent is zero.
Randomized approximation is established, while checked 2026 deterministic results have dimension-dependent error factors or fixed density and weight restrictions.
A complete Lean proof must establish the unrestricted deterministic scheme or prove that none meets the stated guarantees.
